metadata.title: Is The Lift Real?
metadata.description: A CLI-explainer for Sanjana on a core product-management trap: reading an A/B test before it's statistically real. Build a significance check with Claude — show the prompt, the real two-proportion z-test code, and the confidence intervals shrinking as the sample grows until the verdict flips. Framework-first, one revision, falsifiability, scaffolded task. Watermarked @HumanitariansAI.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN — composer, Sanjana greeting, @HumanitariansAI chrome
beats.narration_text: Hi, this is Liam for Sanjana, and this video is about a trap every product manager walks into — calling an A B test a win before it's actually real.

props.command: claude "variant B converted two points higher — should we ship it?"
output: but is it signal or noise?

beats.role_note: the stakes, then the framework shown as a STRUCTURE before any example

qc.sparse_reason: Framework card: three chips (lift + sample size + noise) on cream, shown before any example, like a title card; edge-bleed and contrast still enforced.

beats.narration_text: Here's the trap. Variant B is up two points — a twenty percent lift — and everyone wants to ship. But with a small sample, that gap can be pure noise, and if you ship on noise you spend the next quarter chasing a result that was never there. So here's the frame. Whether a result is real depends on three things: the size of the lift, the size of your sample, and the noise in the data. Put them together as a confidence interval. And the rule that saves you: if the two intervals overlap, you don't have a result yet.

props.title: THE FRAMEWORK
props.caption: Overlapping intervals? Not a result yet.

beats.narration_text: Let's build it with Claude. We have the two conversion rates. First pass — the move everyone makes: just ask which one converted higher.

props.command:
claude "which converted higher — control or variant B?
  report the lift"

beats.narration_text: Read it before you trust it. All it does is divide conversions by users for each arm and take the ratio. Ten percent versus twelve — a twenty percent lift. True arithmetic. But it's a number, not a verdict.

props.title: abtest.py
props.code:
c = 100 / 1000   # control:  10.0%
v = 120 / 1000   # variant:  12.0%

print(f"variant +{(v/c - 1)*100:.0f}% — ship it?")
# +20%. looks like a clear win —
# but is it signal, or noise?

beats.role_note: MOVING output — ABTestBoard, raw bars, no CI (the trap)
beats.narration_text: Run it. Two bars, a plus twenty percent, and a very tempting ship button. This is exactly where most teams stop — and exactly where they get fooled. Nothing here tells you whether that gap would survive a second thousand users.

Here's the fix. Don't just compare — test it. Iterate: run a two-proportion z-test, give me the ninety-five percent confidence interval and the p-value, and tell me the sample size I'd need to trust this.

props.command:
claude "is it significant? two-proportion z-test,
  95% CI and p-value, and the sample size
  we'd need for 80% power"

beats.narration_text: Now the real test. Pool the two rates, get the standard error, and the z-score is the lift divided by that error. Turn z into a p-value. Two points on a thousand users gives p equals zero-point-one-five — and the sample you'd actually need is about thirty-eight hundred per arm.

props.title: abtest.py
props.code:
from math import sqrt, erf
def phi(z): return 0.5*(1 + erf(z/sqrt(2)))

pool = (100 + 120) / (1000 + 1000)
se = sqrt(pool*(1-pool) * (1/1000 + 1/1000))
z  = (0.12 - 0.10) / se
p  = 2 * (1 - phi(abs(z)))   # 0.153 -> not yet
# need ~3,835 / arm for 80% power

beats.role_note: MOVING output — ABTestBoard, CI whiskers shrink as n grows, verdict flips
beats.narration_text: Re-run — and watch what honesty looks like. At a thousand per arm the confidence intervals are wide and they overlap: p is zero-point-one-five, not significant, and you'd need about thirty-eight hundred per arm. So keep the test running. As the sample climbs, the intervals tighten — and only when they finally pull apart does the verdict flip to significant, p zero-point-zero-zero-five. Same lift the whole time. The only thing that changed is how much you're allowed to believe it.

props.title: PASS 2 · 95% CONFIDENCE
props.caption: Same lift — now you can believe it.

beats.narration_text: So the method is one habit that will save you from shipping ghosts: before you read a test, decide the sample size — then check significance, not just the gap. Two honest limits. Don't peek: if you keep checking and stop the moment it crosses the line, you manufacture false wins — fix the sample size up front. And significant is not the same as important: at a huge sample a trivial lift can be real and still not worth building.

props.title: THE METHOD
props.caption: Size the test first. Significant ≠ important.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF — suggested prompt typed in, read aloud; addressed to Sanjana
beats.narration_text: Your turn, Sanjana. Take your own experiment — conversions and users for each arm — paste this prompt, and let Claude run the z-test, hand you the confidence interval and p-value, and tell you the sample size you need and whether to keep running. Decide that number before you look, and you'll never ship a ghost again.

props.command:
claude "here are my A/B results (control: conv/n,
  variant: conv/n). Run a two-proportion z-test,
  give the 95% CI and p-value, the sample size for
  80% power, and whether I should keep running."
